absent: Locking and concurrency rules for LPI and table management are not shown.
Full struct definitions for ITS nodes, BASER descriptors and redistributor state are not shown.
Exported cross-file interfaces beyond file-local helpers are not shown.
Runtime interrupt dispatch, masking, acknowledgement and affinity changes are not shown.

findings.text: Distributor type register encodes LPI identifier width in a five-bit field starting near bit nineteen; architectural value is that field plus one.
ITS table descriptor register encodes table kind in a three-bit type field at its defined shift.
ITS table descriptor encodes per-entry size in a five-bit field; architectural size is field value plus one.
Conversion between 52-bit physical address and 48-bit BASER address field preserves low bits and folds high nibble into defined position.
Reverse conversion from BASER address field to full physical address restores low bits and expands stored high nibble to upper position.
BASER page count is low eight-bit field plus one.
Alignment test checks that address has no remainder modulo power-of-two boundary.
LPI identifier allocator tolerates shortage by repeatedly halving requested count until success or exhaustion, returns zeroed bitmap accounting on success, and clears outputs on any failure.

Property table memory is initialized to a uniform default combining standard priority with group one and disabled state, then made visible to the distributor through cache maintenance to point of coherency.

Validation of firmware-reserved memory accepts any range under crash-dump kernels, otherwise requires containment within a reserved memory entry, warning and tainting on mismatch; reservation delegates to firmware persistent reservation when configuration tables exist.

Property table establishment follows two modes: reuse of firmware preallocated table discovered via redistributor register with identifier width derived from hardware, or fresh allocation limited by distributor capability and ITS maximum, with reservation for persistence.
ITS table kinds include device tables, virtual CPU tables and interrupt collections, with several reserved values retained for architectural extension.
BASER register index derives from position of descriptor within per-ITS table array, with each register spaced by eight bytes from the base.

Table programming guarantees bounded page count, node-local zeroed backing, address-width compatibility tied to page granularity, and sticky attribute programming with shareability reconciliation; violations release backing and report failure.

Two-level table use is considered only when flat size exceeds twice the ITS page size, with hardware support probed by attempting indirect mode; level-one sizing accounts for second-level fan-out and overall order is clamped to maximum page order with identifier width reduced accordingly.

Common LPI affinity masks redistributor affinity by clearing low bytes according to common-affinity level, and ITS affinity is computed by re-encoding its saved affinity and shared-entry support in the same form.

Virtual processing-element table sharing is allowed only among version 4.1 ITS nodes advertising shared-entry support with matching affinity and a valid second table; redistributor inheritance similarly requires matching affinity across possible CPUs and reuses peer mask and owning ITS reference.
Supported page size is the largest among 64K, 16K and 4K that persists after programming; failure occurs when none persists.

Per-ITS bring-up guarantees that empty slots stay untouched, active slots receive probed page size and appropriate flat or indirect sizing with sibling reuse where allowed, cache and shareability choices propagate across tables, and any failure leaves no partial tables.

Virtual level-one table prefers reuse from a matching redistributor, then from a matching ITS, before fresh allocation; fresh tables use probed page size with flat or indirect layout covering the full identifier space, with zeroed memory, validity and sharing-mask membership guaranteed on success.
Second-level virtual backing exists on demand with flat bounds enforcement and indirect index derivation; empty entries gain zeroed pages with coherency maintenance and ordering before hardware use.

Collection storage is allocated per possible CPU with target addresses preset to an invalid all-ones value; pending tables are allocated zeroed and flushed for hardware visibility, with symmetric release.
Early initialization entry establishes the LPI property table and identifier allocator before ITS table use.

Missing reserved-range description taints the kernel; mismatched shareability or non-sticky programming indicates unsupported attributes; high-address allocation without required granularity and oversized identifier spaces trigger truncation warnings rather than silent corruption.
